raw_case_text:
A 76-year-old female patient presented with chest and back pain accompanied by fever, approximately 38.2 C, about 1 month prior to hospital admission, with normal limb mobility at that time. The local hospital initially diagnosed her with gallstones and cholecystitis, and she underwent cholecystectomy and received anti-infective treatment. Post-surgery, her temperature improved, but the pain persisted. She revisited the local hospital due to unrelieved pain, where she was considered to have a gastric ulcer and was treated with proton pump inhibitors among other medications, yet without symptom improvement. Two days before presenting to our hospital for further treatment, the patient experienced a gradual decrease in bilateral lower limb strength. During her stay, she had intermittent fever, peaking around 38.2 C, with no significant gastrointestinal symptoms. Emergency CT indicated a thoracic vertebral fracture at T6/T7 (Figure 1), suspected to be caused by vertebral infection. Subsequently, the patient was admitted to the orthopedics department. Physical examination upon admission revealed normal development, good nutritional status, natural facial expression, and moderate body build. The patient was alert and cooperative during the examination, with primary positive findings including loss of pain and touch sensation below the level of the xiphoid process, grade 0 strength in both lower limbs, positive bilateral Babinski sign, loss of saddle area touch sensation, and absence of the anal reflex. Admission tests showed a white blood cell count of 15.41x10^9/L, monocytes at 0.881x10^9/L, lymphocytes at 2.01x10^9/L, neutrophils at 12.971x10^9/L, C-reactive protein at 131.8 mg/L, and a temperature of 37.4 C. Considering the patient's test results and local epidemiological investigation, the diagnosis was considered to be an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and a treatment regimen primarily consisting of anti-tuberculosis drugs (levofloxacin, isoniazid, amikacin, rifampicin, ethionamide, and pyrazinamide) was initiated. Concurrently, related surgical examinations were completed, and on the third day of admission, surgery was performed (posterior spinal canal decompression with internal fixation by pedicle screw and lateral bone grafting), along with the placement of a wound drainage tube, and the excised tissue was sent for culture. Based on intraoperative findings, the doctor suspected a Staphylococcus aureus infection, and the anti-infective treatment regimen was adjusted to cefoperazone-sulbactam plus vancomycin.
On the fourth day of admission, 65 reads were identified as Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and 19 reads were identified as Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, and this result was also supported by the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) verification. Based on the results of domestic epidemiological investigations, the anti-infection treatment plan was adjusted to ceftriaxone. The patient's temperature and inflammatory markers showed a trend of improvement, and she was subsequently transferred to a local hospital for continued treatment. Approximately 6 months later, follow-up revealed no fever, and stool culture and agglutination tests were negative, and no clinical sign of recurrence was observed in the spine (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old female presented with a 1-month history of chest and back pain accompanied by intermittent fever (up to 38.2 °C) and a 2-day progressive loss of bilateral lower limb strength.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Approximately 1 month prior to admission, the patient developed chest and back pain with fever around 38.2 °C and normal limb mobility. At a local hospital, she was diagnosed with gallstones and cholecystitis and underwent cholecystectomy with anti-infective therapy; her fever transiently improved, but chest and back pain persisted. On re-evaluation at the local hospital, she was treated with proton pump inhibitors for a suspected gastric ulcer without relief. Two days prior to admission at our hospital, she developed progressive bilateral lower limb weakness. During hospitalization, she had intermittent fevers peaking at ~38.2 °C without significant gastrointestinal symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with gallstones and cholecystitis 1 month prior to admission and underwent cholecystectomy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chest pain, back pain, intermittent fever, and progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness/paralysis. Pertinent negative: no significant gastrointestinal symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, temperature was 37.4 °C. The patient was alert and cooperative with normal development, good nutritional status, natural facial expression, and moderate body build. Neurological examination revealed complete paraplegia with grade 0/5 muscle strength in both lower limbs, loss of pain and touch sensation below the level of the xiphoid process, loss of saddle-area touch sensation, absent anal reflex, and bilateral positive Babinski signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests showed leukocytosis with WBC 15.41 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 12.971 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 2.01 x 10^9/L, monocytes 0.881 x 10^9/L, and elevated C-reactive protein at 131.8 mg/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Emergency thoracic CT demonstrated a T6/T7 vertebral fracture with destruction suspicious for infectious spondylodiscitis. On hospital day 3, she underwent posterior spinal canal decompression, pedicle screw internal fixation, lateral bone grafting, and wound drainage tube placement, with excised vertebral tissue submitted for microbiological and molecular analysis. On hospital day 4, metagenomic sequencing and confirmatory PCR of the surgical specimen identified 65 reads of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and 19 reads of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Thoracic vertebral osteomyelitis/spondylodiscitis (T6/T7) with pathological fracture and spinal cord compression caused by mixed Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi infection, confirmed by metagenomic sequencing (65 reads S. Typhimurium, 19 reads S. Typhi) and PCR verification of excised spinal tissue. Initial clinical suspicions of spinal tuberculosis (treated empirically with levofloxacin, isoniazid, amikacin, rifampicin, ethionamide, and pyrazinamide) and intraoperative suspicion of Staphylococcus aureus (treated with cefoperazone-sulbactam plus vancomycin) were revised once Salmonella PCR/sequencing results returned on day 4. Following surgical decompression, internal fixation, and adjustment of antimicrobial therapy to intravenous ceftriaxone, her fever and inflammatory markers improved, and she was transferred to a local hospital to complete therapy. At 6-month follow-up, she remained afebrile with negative stool cultures, negative agglutination tests, and no clinical or radiological recurrence in the spine.
